title: Abraham Dies; Twins Struggle; a Birthright Sold
summary: Abraham's sons by Keturah are listed and sent east, and Abraham dies at 175 and is buried beside Sarah by Isaac and Ishmael. Ishmael's twelve sons are named. Then Isaac's story begins: after twenty years of barrenness Rebekah conceives twins who struggle in the womb, God tells her the older will serve the younger, and Esau, famished, sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.
story: The chapter is a hinge between generations. It closes Abraham's life, gives Ishmael's line its due, and opens the story of Isaac's family, which will run through Genesis 35. The promises now pass to Isaac, and the first thing the new story shows is that the same pattern holds: a barren wife, a prayer, a birth that only God can give. It also introduces the conflict that will shape the next ten chapters, the rivalry between Jacob and Esau, and a divine word that turns the expected order upside down. Jacob, not Esau, will carry the promise, and the question of how he comes to it will dominate what follows.
historical:
Many of the names in this chapter belong to peoples of northern and western Arabia and the desert fringes east and south of Canaan. Midian, a son of Keturah, gives his name to the Midianites, among whom Moses will later live (Exodus 2:15). Sheba and Dedan were Arabian peoples associated with caravan trade. Among Ishmael's sons, Kedar and Nebaioth are known from Assyrian records of the eighth and seventh centuries BC, which mention the Qedarites as a powerful Arab tribal group, and Tema and Dumah correspond to the Arabian oases of Tayma and Dumat al-Jandal. Genesis presents these peoples as distant relatives of Israel, all descended from Abraham.

Esau is identified with Edom (verse 30), the land and people southeast of the Dead Sea who would be Israel's neighbors and frequent rivals. The oracle that “two nations are in your womb” (verse 23) looks forward to that later history. The chronology of the chapter also rewards attention. Abraham was a hundred at Isaac's birth and Isaac sixty at the twins' birth, so Abraham actually lived until Jacob and Esau were fifteen. The narrator finishes Abraham's story before beginning theirs.
cultural:
The birthright was the firstborn son's privilege: a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17) and leadership of the family after the father's death. In Abraham's family it also meant carrying the covenant promises. Such rights could apparently be transferred; a tablet from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia records a man selling his inheritance share to his brother in exchange for sheep. Esau's sale is legally binding because it is sealed with an oath.

The names carry meaning. Esau came out red and hairy; red in Hebrew sounds like Edom, and hairy sounds like Seir, the hill country where Edom lived. Jacob came out grasping his brother's heel, and his name sounds like the Hebrew word for heel, with overtones of overreaching or supplanting that Esau will draw out later (Genesis 27:36). Parental favoritism, Isaac loving Esau and Rebekah loving Jacob (verse 28), plants the conflict that erupts in Genesis 27. Keturah is called a wife here and a concubine in 1 Chronicles 1:32; the gifts Abraham gives to his other sons before sending them away (verse 6) make clear that Isaac alone is the heir.
literary: Genesis is organized by a series of headings that the BSB translates “This is the account” (Hebrew toledot, generations or family history). Two appear here: the account of Ishmael (verse 12) and the account of Isaac (verse 19). The pattern is typical: the line not chosen is treated briefly and respectfully, then set aside, and the chosen line receives the long story. Ishmael's twelve princes fulfill God's promise in Genesis 17:20. The birth story is full of wordplay, and the oracle of verse 23 is poetry, four lines in two pairs. The birthright scene is told almost entirely in short speeches and ends with a rapid string of verbs, “ate and drank and then got up and went away”, before the narrator's verdict: “Thus Esau despised his birthright.”

outline.t: The death and burial of Abraham
Isaac's prayer and the birth of Esau and Jacob

doctrines.note: Before the twins are born, God declares that “the older will serve the younger” (verse 23). Paul uses this in Romans 9:10-13 to teach that God's purposes rest on his calling, not on human achievement or birth order. How to understand election is debated; see the hard question.

Isaac prays for his barren wife, and “the LORD heard his prayer” (verse 21), though the twins arrive twenty years after the wedding. Rebekah, troubled by the struggle within her, goes “to inquire of the LORD” (verse 22). Both bring their need directly to God.

Esau trades something lasting for immediate appetite, and the narrator calls it contempt. Jacob, for his part, exploits his brother's hunger. Neither brother looks good here; God's choice of Jacob is not a reward for better behavior.

words.note: Bekorah, birthright: the rights of the firstborn son, related to the word for firstborn. It included a larger share of the inheritance and the headship of the family. The same letters, rearranged, spell the word for blessing (berakah), and the two will be joined in Genesis 27.

Bazah, to despise or treat as worthless. The narrator's closing word on Esau is not that he was cheated but that he despised what he had. Hebrews 12:16 draws on this, calling Esau godless because for a single meal he sold his birthright.

Asaph, to gather. Abraham and Ishmael are each “gathered to his people” (verses 8 and 17). The phrase is distinct from burial, since Abraham is buried far from his ancestors, and many see in it an early hint that death does not end a person's existence or belonging.

Aqev, heel. Jacob is born grasping Esau's heel, and his name echoes the word. The related verb means to take by the heel, to overreach or supplant, and the prophet Hosea recalls that in the womb Jacob took his brother by the heel (Hosea 12:3).

christ: Paul reads the oracle to Rebekah as a key to how God works: before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, she was told, “The older will serve the younger,” so that God's purpose would rest “not by works but by Him who calls” (Romans 9:11-12). Genesis repeatedly shows God choosing the younger or the unexpected: Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim, and later David. That pattern prepares for the gospel, in which God's grace comes to those with no claim on it and Jesus says that the last will be first. The link is thematic rather than predictive. The chapter also continues the line of promise through Isaac and now Jacob, the ancestor of Israel's twelve tribes and of David's royal house, from which the Messiah comes. And Hebrews 12:16-17 uses Esau as a warning to Christians not to trade their inheritance in Christ for what satisfies only for a moment.

hard.q: Did God choose Jacob and reject Esau before they were born?
hard.a:
Verse 23 declares the outcome before the twins' birth, and Paul, quoting Malachi 1:2-3, writes, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13). Christians have read this in different ways, and the question of election is one where faithful traditions disagree.

In the Augustinian and Reformed reading, Paul uses Jacob and Esau to show that God's choice of individuals for salvation rests entirely on his free mercy, not on anything foreseen in them. In Arminian and Wesleyan readings, and in many others, the oracle concerns nations and roles in history (“Two nations are in your womb”), and Paul's point in Romans 9 is that God is free to choose the line through which he will work, including Gentiles, without that being a verdict on each person's eternal destiny. Many on both sides note that loved and hated in Hebrew idiom can express choosing one over another rather than emotional hatred (compare Genesis 29:30-31). Genesis itself doesn't treat Esau as beyond God's care: he prospers, his descendants become a nation, and Israel is later told not to despise an Edomite, “for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

questions: Esau traded a lasting inheritance for an immediate craving. What long-term goods are most at risk when you are tired, hungry, or pressured?
Isaac and Rebekah each had a favorite son. What does this chapter suggest about the effects of favoritism in a family?
God chose Jacob before he had done anything good or bad. How does that shape the way you think about your own standing before God?
